question: What is the exact universal vessel-noise threshold above which every humpback whale becomes completely unable to communicate?
expected_gold_answer: No such universal threshold can be derived from Dunlop (2019) or the other included studies. Communication range varies with signal frequency, background sound, propagation, behavioural context and assumptions about hearing; Dunlop’s ranges are model-based rather than a universal complete-silence cutoff.
required_facts: ["Refuse to provide an exact universal dB threshold.", "Explain dependence on acoustic context and model assumptions."]
forbidden_claims: ["Turn 105 or 110 dB re 1 µPa into a universal cutoff."]
model_response: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE: None of the provided passages states an exact, universal vessel-noise level above which every humpback whale is completely unable to communicate. The excerpts report reduced communication space, modelling approaches (e.g. using signal-to-noise assumptions), or use context-specific thresholds (e.g. a 15 dB background threshold in one study), but do not provide an empirical, universally applicable noise threshold that causes complete communication loss for all humpback whales. question: In Blair et al. (2016), what changes in foraging were associated with increased ship noise for tagged humpback whales?
expected_gold_answer: In 10 tagged, bottom-foraging humpback whales, increasing ship noise was associated with slower descent rates and fewer side-roll feeding events per dive. Five of 18 ship passages included no-side-roll dives. The study assessed within-dive behaviour, not population survival.
required_facts: ["10 tagged foraging whales.", "Slower descent rate.", "Fewer side-roll feeding events per dive.", "Five of eighteen ship passages included no-roll dives."]
forbidden_claims: ["Measured whale population decline or reproductive success."]
model_response:
- Increased ship noise was associated with reduced (slower) feeding-dive descent rates. [P04 p.1] [P04 p.4]
- Increased ship noise was associated with a decrease in the number of bottom-feeding events per dive. [P04 p.4]
- Ship passages were correlated with dives without bottom side-rolls (fewer side-roll feeding events per dive), implying a cessation of bottom-side-roll feeding or a switch to another feeding method. [P04 p.4] [P04 p.1]

question: Following the September 2001 shipping reduction in the Bay of Fundy, what acoustic and physiological changes did Rolland et al. (2012) report?
expected_gold_answer: The researchers found roughly a 6 dB reduction in overall underwater noise and a significant decline in noise below 150 Hz, accompanied by lower baseline faecal glucocorticoid metabolite levels in North Atlantic right whales. The comparison was a retrospective natural experiment, not a randomised causal trial.

forbidden_claims: ["Stress-hormone decline proves ship noise caused every stress response."]
model_response:
- Acoustic: underwater background noise in the Bay of Fundy decreased by about 6 dB after the September 2001 reduction in ship traffic, with significant reductions at frequencies below 150 Hz (notably 50–150 Hz) and a shift of the peak noise frequency to higher frequencies. [P06 p.1] [P06 p.3] [P06 p.3]
- Physiological: baseline concentrations of faecal glucocorticoid metabolites (fGCs) in North Atlantic right whales decreased after the post‑9/11 reduction in underwater noise (the post‑9/11 decrease in fGCs was reported as highly significant compared with other years). [P06 p.1] [P06 p.3] [P06 p.3]
